title: Models · Agents
description: Understand inference, tool execution and feedback by following one debugging investigation across the boundary between a model and its environment.

sections.title: The part of the problem the model cannot see

blocks.body:
Imagine a small helper that retries an operation after it fails. A test calls it with the number 2. The operation fails twice and would succeed on its third call, but the helper gives up after the second. The test expected success.

You send that description to a model and ask for a diagnosis. It suggests an off-by-one error: perhaps the loop stops one attempt too early. That is a sensible hypothesis. Yet there is a question hiding inside it: what does the number 2 mean?

It could mean **two attempts in total**, or **two retries after an initial attempt**. Those conventions produce different correct implementations. If the argument is a retry count, the test may have exposed a bug. If it is a total-attempt count, the test may be wrong. A confident explanation of the loop does not settle the contract.

Picture two repositories side by side. Their failing test output is identical, but their API documentation specifies different conventions. A model given only that output receives exactly the same evidence in both cases. It can use familiar naming conventions to make a reasonable guess, but it cannot reliably identify which repository it is in. The missing distinction is outside its input.

This gives us a useful starting point for agentic engineering. Before asking whether a model is clever enough to solve a problem, identify what would make the problem solvable from the information available. Sometimes the next useful step is further reasoning. Here, it is an observation: read the contract and the code that uses it.

blocks.question: What would you inspect first to decide whether the helper or the test is wrong?
blocks.answer: Look for the intended meaning of the argument: API documentation, established callers and relevant tests. Reading the loop tells you what the program does; the contract tells you what it should do. If these sources disagree, the disagreement itself needs resolving before a patch can be called correct.

blocks.body: For the rest of this investigation, suppose the repository confirms that 2 means two retries after the first attempt. Now we have something more useful than a plausible diagnosis: a claim that can be checked against a particular implementation. The model did not acquire that fact by being encouraged to sound more certain. Something supplied new evidence.

sections.title: What happens inside one model call?

blocks.body:
A language model brings learned capabilities to the investigation. During training, its numerical parameters are adjusted. Those parameters can encode patterns that help it interpret language, follow code, recognise familiar mistakes and carry out multi-step reasoning. During an ordinary inference call, we use those learned parameters without updating them.

The other ingredient is the input for this call: the task, instructions, conversation and any evidence the surrounding application includes. We will call that input the **context**. The repository may contain a million lines, but a file sitting on disk does not influence a call merely because it exists. Its contents must reach the model through some input path.

In a typical text-generating language model, text is represented as tokens—pieces of text, often shorter than words. Generation proceeds by producing tokens conditioned on the input and the output already produced. That describes a computational interface, not a ceiling on the complexity of the work: a generated sequence can contain an argument, a program or a carefully chosen request for more information. A separate later stage of training, often built from human feedback on example conversations, can also shape how a model follows instructions, stays inside a stated role or declines an unsafe request. That is still a change made before this conversation began; it explains why the model behaves the way it does, not how the current call itself works.

For our purposes, the key boundary is easier to see from the outside. One inference call takes supplied information and produces output. That output can be an explanation of the retry bug, a proposed patch or a structured request to read a file. None of those outputs, by itself, changes the repository.

You can see the distinction by disconnecting the surrounding application from the filesystem. The model may still produce exactly the patch it would have produced before. The file on disk remains untouched. Conversely, a small program can apply a supplied patch without using a model at all. Deciding on an edit and executing it are separate operations, even when a product presents them in one smooth conversation.

This also explains a common source of confusion about learning. Once the model is shown the retry contract, a later response can use it. The ordinary explanation is that the fact is now in the input, not that the call retrained the model. An application may save that fact and retrieve it in a future session; that is another mechanism again. We will follow it in chapter three.

sections.title: Let the model ask for the missing piece

data.title: The return path changes the next decision
data.caption: Start at the upper left. The model proposes a request; the surrounding program executes it. The observation returns through the lower path and becomes input to a later call. Cut that return path and the model cannot adapt to what the tool found.

blocks.body:
Now continue the retry investigation. Reading the implementation shows a loop that makes two calls when the contract allows three. The model proposes a change, a file-editing tool applies it, and the model requests a focused test. We have reached a branch in the investigation: the test result should determine what happens next.

If the test reaches the assertion and still reports two calls, the proposed change has not fixed the observed behaviour. Perhaps the edited function is not the one the test imports. Reading that import is now more informative than adjusting the loop again. If the command exits before running any tests because a fixture is missing, there is no new evidence about the loop at all. The sensible next action concerns test setup.

These two failures could both produce a nonzero exit code. Their meanings are different. A useful system returns enough of the observation for the model to distinguish them: which command ran, where it ran, whether tests started, and what failed. “Command failed” throws away much of the information that could make the next step better.

When the corrected helper passes the original test, we can ask a second question that the first test does not answer: what happens when zero retries are allowed? The initial attempt should still happen. If the operation fails on that attempt, the helper should propagate the error without a second call. This boundary case is valuable because it separates a fix to the counting convention from a change that merely makes one example pass.

The sequence has become a feedback loop. The next action depends on the previous observation; the entire route need not be known in advance. This is the operational meaning of **agent** we will use in the course: a system in which a model chooses actions within an action–observation loop. The term has other uses, so it is worth keeping this definition attached to the behaviour rather than to a product label.

A scripted pipeline can also read a file, edit it and run a test. The distinction is where decisions about the route live. In a fixed pipeline, the programmer has specified the branches ahead of time. In this agent loop, the model can decide that a surprising import, an absent fixture or a new failing assertion deserves investigation. Real systems often combine fixed workflow stages with model-directed work inside a stage.

sections.title: Why another turn can help—and why it sometimes doesn't

blocks.body:
The benefit of a loop is the opportunity to change the information available. Think back to the two possible meanings of the retry count. Reading the contract removed an ambiguity. Reading the implementation located a mismatch. Running a boundary test challenged the proposed repair. Each action made a later decision better grounded.

Repeating a command can be useful when its outcome is expected to vary—for example, when investigating an intermittent failure. It contributes little when a deterministic setup error makes it stop at the same point every time. After three identical “fixture not found” results, a fourth call needs a reason. The existence of unused turns is not such a reason.

This suggests a practical way to read an agent trace. At each action, ask what uncertainty it could reduce or what justified change it could make. You do not need access to private internal reasoning to inspect the connection between the visible request, the evidence returned and the next operation. A trace that keeps circling the same failure without changing its investigation is showing a system problem, even if every individual response reads fluently.

The same perspective improves comparisons. If two assistants use the same model but only one finds the current implementation, their results are not a clean comparison of model capability. Their context, tools or execution environments differ. Hold the task and relevant conditions steady, change the suspected cause, and repeat enough trials to distinguish a real improvement from run-to-run variation. One successful rerun is a useful clue, not a general benchmark.

blocks.question: The tool applied a patch and returned “success”. Which uncertainty has that removed, and which uncertainties remain?
blocks.answer: It supports the claim that the edit operation completed under the tool's contract. You still need to inspect the resulting change and obtain evidence about its behaviour. The edit may target the wrong file, implement the wrong convention or introduce another failure. A passing focused test narrows those uncertainties further; it does not establish every property of the program.

sections.title: The run ends; the evidence tells us how

blocks.body:
An agent loop could keep finding more things to investigate. A task therefore needs a boundary around both its purpose and its resources. For this repair, the purpose might be to restore the documented retry-count behaviour, check success and exhaustion, and leave a reviewable diff. Resource limits might cap elapsed time, model calls or tool execution.

Those boundaries answer different questions. The acceptance evidence tells us whether the requested result was obtained. The budget tells us how much work the system may spend trying. Reaching a call limit cannot turn an unfinished patch into a completed repair. A run may finish successfully, stop because it lacks a required capability, or exhaust its budget while uncertainty remains. A useful report preserves that distinction.

Nor does more autonomy automatically improve the task. If all we need is an explanation of a supplied ten-line function, a single model call may be enough. The loop earns its complexity when the system needs to discover evidence, act on it and respond to consequences. A person can supervise each step, delegate a bounded investigation, or eventually arrange for such investigations to start automatically. These choices change how work is initiated and supervised; they do not remove the need for evidence.

We can now look at a coding assistant and see several operations that its interface blends together: a model interpreting context, a program performing requested actions, and observations informing another decision. The next chapter opens up that surrounding program. If the model proposes a sensible action, what must be true for the action to happen reliably—and for the result to mean what the model thinks it means?

heading: How does a model become something that can act?
lead: Follow a small debugging problem from a plausible answer to an observed result. The change happens when we give the model a way to ask the world a question—and let the answer change what it does next.
outcomes: Explain what changes during inference and what remains in the surrounding system.
Trace a tool request through execution and back into the next decision.
Distinguish a useful observation, a verified result and a reason to stop.
